title: Chapter 7 — The Chapel
paragraphs: In this same New Bedford stands a Whaleman's Chapel, and few moody fishermen, shortly bound for the Indian Ocean or Pacific, fail to pay it a Sunday visit. I certainly didn't.

Returning from my morning stroll, I set out on this particular errand. The sky had changed from clear, sunny cold to driving sleet and mist. Wrapping myself in my shaggy bearskin jacket, I fought my way through the stubborn storm. Inside, I found a small, scattered congregation of sailors and sailors' wives and widows. A muffled silence reigned, broken only by shrieks of the storm. Each worshipper seemed deliberately sitting apart from the others, as if each grief were an island, incommunicable. The chaplain hadn't arrived yet. These silent islands of men and women sat steadfastly gazing at several marble tablets with black borders, set into the walls on either side of the pulpit. Three of them read something like this, though I don't pretend to quote exactly:

SACRED TO THE MEMORY OF JOHN TALBOT, Who, at the age of eighteen, was lost overboard, Near the Isle of Desolation, off Patagonia, November 1st, 1836. THIS TABLET Is erected to his Memory BY HIS SISTER.

SACRED TO THE MEMORY OF ROBERT LONG, WILLIS ELLERY, NATHAN COLEMAN, WALTER CANNY, SETH MACY, AND SAMUEL GLEIG, Forming one of the boats' crews OF THE SHIP ELIZA Who were towed out of sight by a Whale, On the Off-shore Ground in the PACIFIC, December 31st, 1839. THIS MARBLE Is here placed by their surviving SHIPMATES.

SACRED TO THE MEMORY OF The late CAPTAIN EZEKIEL HARDY, Who in the bows of his boat was killed by a Sperm Whale on the coast of Japan, August 3d, 1833. THIS TABLET Is erected to his Memory BY HIS WIDOW.

Shaking the sleet from my ice-glazed hat and jacket, I sat down near the door and was surprised to see Queequeg nearby. Moved by the solemnity of the scene, he wore a look of wondering, incredulous curiosity. He was the only person who seemed to notice my arrival — because he was the only one who couldn't read, and therefore wasn't reading those cold inscriptions on the wall. Whether any of the dead sailors' relatives were in the congregation, I didn't know. But so many are the unrecorded accidents in the whale fishery, and so plainly did several women present wear the look of unceasing grief, that I felt sure these were people in whose unhealed hearts the sight of those bleak tablets made old wounds bleed fresh.

Oh, you whose dead lie buried beneath green grass, who can stand among flowers and say, 'Here lies my beloved' — you don't know the desolation that haunts hearts like these. What bitter blanks in those black-bordered marble tablets that cover no ashes! What despair in those immovable inscriptions! What deadly emptiness in lines that seem to gnaw at all Faith, refusing resurrection to those who have perished without a place, without a grave. Those tablets might as well stand in the caves of Elephanta.

In what census of living creatures are the dead of mankind included? Why does the universal proverb say the dead tell no tales, though they contain more secrets than the Goodwin Sands? Why do we prefix such a significant and faithless word to the name of someone who departed yesterday for the other world, yet don't use that word for someone who merely embarks for the remotest shores of this living earth? Why do life insurance companies pay death-claims on supposedly immortal souls? In what eternal, unstirring paralysis lies ancient Adam, who died sixty centuries ago? Why do we refuse to be comforted for those we insist are dwelling in unspeakable bliss? Why do the living strive so hard to silence the dead? Why does the mere rumor of a knocking in a tomb terrify an entire city? All these things have their meanings.
But Faith, like a jackal, feeds among the tombs, and even from these dead doubts she gathers her most vital hope.

I hardly need to describe with what feelings, on the eve of a Nantucket voyage, I gazed at those marble tablets and read — by the murky light of that dark, doleful day — the fate of whalemen who had gone before me. Yes, Ishmael, the same fate could be yours. But somehow I grew cheerful again. Delightful inducements to go whaling! Fine chance for advancement, it seems — a smashed boat will make me immortal by reputation. Yes, there is death in this whaling business — a speechlessly quick, chaotic bundling of a man into Eternity. But what of it? I think we've made a tremendous mistake about this matter of Life and Death. I think what they call my shadow here on earth is my true substance. I think that in looking at spiritual things, we're too much like oysters observing the sun through water, thinking the thick water is the thinnest air. My body is just the dregs of my better being. Take my body, whoever wants it — take it, I say — it is not me. And so three cheers for Nantucket; and let the boat be smashed and the body staved when they will, for stave my soul, Jove himself cannot.
